speakers.role: Consultant in Paediatric Emergency Medicine

summary: A review of a paediatric transport service looking at ambulance mileage, family travel distances and environmental impact after GIRFT recommendations.
description:
Dr Nadia Audhali, Consultant in Paediatric Emergency Medicine, provides insights into a review of a paediatric transport service following GIRFT recommendations for care closer to home. She discusses the relationship between regional care pathways, ambulance mileage and the distances families travel when children need intensive care. The interview explores findings on transport use, fuel consumption and environmental impact, and how these relate to wider NHS priorities around sustainability and value. Dr Audhali also considers the potential benefit for families, while noting that the study examined travel data rather than directly measuring families' experiences through qualitative interviews.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Why population data matter in paediatric critical care

speakers.name: Sarah Seaton
speakers.role: Associate Professor at the University of Leicester and co-lead of the Paediatric Intensive Care Audit Network

summary: How population-level data such as PICANet can reveal problems earlier and guide research priorities in paediatric critical care.
description:
Sarah Seaton, Associate Professor at the University of Leicester and co-lead of the Paediatric Intensive Care Audit Network, provides insights into the importance of population-level data in paediatric critical care. She explains why looking across broad groups of children can help identify challenges that may not be visible when focusing on individual patients or units alone. The interview considers how PICANet and other real-world data sources can guide more focused investigation into particular services, conditions or patient groups. Sarah discusses the potential of these data to reveal problems earlier and help shape research priorities across paediatric critical care.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Caring for children with complex critical illness

speakers.name: Dr Sofia I. Cuevas-Asturias
speakers.role: Consultant in Paediatric Intensive Care

summary: UK mixed-methods work on how children with complex critical illness are defined, supported and cared for by multidisciplinary teams.
description:
Dr Sofia I. Cuevas-Asturias, Consultant in Paediatric Intensive Care, discusses multidisciplinary care for children with complex critical illness. She describes UK mixed-methods work with PICSTAR examining how these children are defined and supported, and how teams organise their care. The interview explores access to specialist resources, different models of multidisciplinary working and the challenges faced by staff. Dr Cuevas-Asturias reflects on areas of growing provision as well as remaining gaps, highlighting the need to consider the experiences of children, families and professionals when developing services.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Behind the scenes of PCCS London 2026

speakers.name: Professor Padmanabhan Ramnarayan
speakers.role: Professor of Paediatric Critical Care at Imperial College London

summary: How the PCCS London 2026 conference was organised, from choosing the venue to building the programme with organisers and volunteers.
description:
Professor Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, Professor of Paediatric Critical Care at Imperial College London, reflects on organising PCCS London 2026 at Lord’s. He discusses choosing the venue, developing the scientific programme and bringing together a broad range of expertise. The interview explores the practical work behind a conference, from logistics to collaboration with event organisers and the contribution of volunteers. Professor Ramnarayan highlights the teamwork involved in creating a meeting for the paediatric critical-care community and the value of providing opportunities for colleagues to learn, exchange ideas and connect.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Putting patient and family voices at the heart of research

speakers.name: Dr Julie Menzies
speakers.role: Clinical Academic Nurse Researcher at Bristol Royal Hospital for Children

summary: How involving patients and families, through a national group and the research incubator, can improve research questions, study design and service evaluation.
description:
Dr Julie Menzies, Clinical Academic Nurse Researcher at Bristol Royal Hospital for Children, discusses the importance of involving patients and families in paediatric critical-care research. She describes work within the paediatric critical-care research incubator and how a national involvement group can help researchers develop early ideas. The interview considers the contribution of lived experience to research questions and study design, as well as audit, quality improvement and service evaluation. Dr Menzies highlights opportunities to make participation a more consistent part of clinical and academic work and to ensure that research reflects what matters to families.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Improving timely treatment of childhood status epilepticus

speakers.name: Dr Natasha Levey
speakers.role: Consultant General Paediatrician

summary: An audit of delays in acute status epilepticus treatment, and quality-improvement ideas such as record prompts, teaching and simulation.
description:
Dr Natasha Levey, Consultant General Paediatrician, provides insights into an audit of the acute management of status epilepticus in children. She discusses the challenges of documenting seizure and treatment timings, and the delays identified when local practice was compared with established guidance. The interview explores plans to broaden the study across additional services and develop a quality-improvement programme. Dr Levey outlines potential interventions, including electronic-record prompts, more reliable time recording, targeted teaching and simulation. She reflects on how these measures could support teams in recognising the time-critical nature of care and identifying where processes need to improve.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Improving high-flow weaning in district general hospitals

speakers.name: Diana Iskander
speakers.role: Paediatric Consultant at William Harvey Hospital

summary: An audit of high-flow weaning against a regional guideline, why practice differed, and the importance of work of breathing alongside oxygen needs.
description:
Diana Iskander, Paediatric Consultant at William Harvey Hospital, discusses a retrospective audit of high-flow weaning in two district general hospitals. She describes reviewing adherence to a regional guideline and examining why practice did not always follow its oxygen-based weaning approach. The interview explores the importance of considering respiratory distress and work of breathing alongside oxygen requirements. Diana reflects on the limitations of the audit, steps taken to improve clinicians’ awareness and changes to local guidance, as well as sharing the findings to inform future guideline development.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Demonstrating the value of critical-care nursing

speakers.name: Dr Julie Menzies
speakers.role: Clinical Academic Nurse Researcher at Bristol Royal Hospital for Children

summary: The gaps in evidence on how registered nursing expertise and staffing affect paediatric critical care, and the research needed to fill them.
description:
Dr Julie Menzies, Clinical Academic Nurse Researcher at Bristol Royal Hospital for Children, explores the contribution of the registered nursing workforce to safe, high-quality paediatric critical care. She discusses gaps in the evidence around staffing and the need to understand more fully how nursing expertise affects care. The interview highlights the importance of appropriate education, specialist training and professional skills, alongside questions about staffing ratios. Dr Menzies reflects on developing research that can demonstrate the value of nurses and help inform decisions about the workforce needed to care for critically ill children.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: NIHR Incubator - supporting paediatric critical care researchers

speakers.name: Professor Padmanabhan Ramnarayan
speakers.role: Professor of Paediatric Critical Care at Imperial College London

summary: How the NIHR research incubator supports new paediatric critical-care researchers with training, mentorship and help developing ideas and grant applications.
description:
Professor Padmanabhan Ramnarayan, Professor of Paediatric Critical Care at Imperial College London, discusses supporting the next generation of paediatric critical-care researchers. He describes the work of the NIHR research incubator, including training, mentorship and help with developing research ideas and grant applications. The interview highlights multidisciplinary participation and the importance of patient and public involvement throughout the research process. Professor Ramnarayan reflects on building a research community, helping colleagues develop their careers and sustaining the collaboration and support created through the incubator.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Community partnership in critical-care research

speakers.name: Riham Lotfi
speakers.role: Community Partner at Imperial College London

summary: What patient and public involvement looks like in practice, including flexibility, co-production and treating community members as research partners.
description:
Riham Lotfi, Community Partner at Imperial College London, shares her experience of patient and public involvement in critical-care research. She discusses the importance of flexibility, mutual learning and making space for both positive and difficult experiences. The interview explores co-production and the value of recognising community participants as partners in the research process. Riham reflects on how lived experience can strengthen research and help ensure that questions and projects remain connected to the people they aim to serve. She highlights the benefits of working together and building research with communities.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Preparing for court: a critical-care clinician’s perspective

speakers.name: Dr Joe Brierley
speakers.role: Consultant Paediatric Intensivist and Director of Paediatric Bioethics at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: Practical advice on preparing to give evidence in court, from witness statements to explaining clinical care clearly while respecting families.
description:
Dr Joe Brierley, Consultant Paediatric Intensivist and Director of Paediatric Bioethics at Great Ormond Street Hospital, provides insights into preparing to give evidence in court. He discusses the role of witness statements, presenting factual information clearly and understanding the questions clinicians may face. The interview considers practical preparation, respectful communication and maintaining constructive relationships with families during difficult proceedings. Dr Brierley reflects on the particular challenges of cases involving life-sustaining treatment and the importance of explaining clinical care in language that the court can understand.

This interview took place at the PCCS Annual Scientific Meeting 2026 in London.

title: Advancing equity for children and young people seeking asylum and refuge: Project AEGIS

speakers.name: Grace Hastie
speakers.role: Policy Manager for Child Protection and Ethics at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health

summary: A NIHR-funded project is bringing together best practice and policy to improve support for children and young people seeking asylum, working with young people.
description: Grace Hastie, Policy Manager for Child Protection and Ethics at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, provides insights into Project AEGIS, an exciting National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) funded project hosted at UCL. The focus of the project is supporting children and young people seeking asylum and refuge. Grace highlights the importance of bringing together best practices and existing policy interventions, while also centering the voices and experiences of young people themselves. She discusses the project’s aims to identify what works, address gaps in support, and design new policy interventions to improve outcomes for these vulnerable groups across the country. Grace emphasises the value of collaboration with young people to ensure meaningful and sustainable change. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Medicines for Children: 20 years of accessible, reliable information for families

speakers.name: Dr Anna Rossiter
speakers.role: Project manager for the Medicines for Children initiative at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health

summary: How a long-running multi-partner website and a parent-held app turn complex medicine information into guidance families can use, and how clinicians can help.
description:
www.medicinesforchildren.org.uk

Dr Anna Rossiter, project manager for the Medicines for Children initiative at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, provides insights into this long-standing, multi-partner project. Founded in 2006, Medicines for Children is a collaboration with the Neonatal and Paediatric Pharmacists Group and the children’s charity WellChild. The project transforms complex medicine information into accessible guidance for families, empowering them to safely administer medicines to their children, even in urgent situations. The website now features over 220 children’s medicines, starting with the most commonly prescribed and expanding to those rarely used but difficult to find information on elsewhere. With approximately 2 million downloads per year globally, the resource is widely used, yet Anna highlights the ongoing need to increase awareness—especially among primary care providers—so that families can be directed to the site when prescriptions are made. The initiative is also creating QR code posters for clinics (such as epilepsy and cardiac clinics) and has launched a parent-held mobile app for children with complex medical needs, currently available on Apple devices. Anna invites clinicians to contribute their expertise to review and expand the information available and to help keep it up to date. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland

title: Supporting patient safety in paediatrics: RCPCH resources and initiatives

speakers.name: Jonathan Bamber
speakers.role: Head of Quality Improvement at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health

summary: An overview of the RCPCH patient safety portal, its podcasts on safety culture and learning from harm, the SAFE programme and a new safety e-bulletin.
description: Jonathan Bamber, Head of Quality Improvement at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, provides insights into the ongoing efforts to support patient safety for children, young people, and RCPCH members. The discussion highlights key initiatives such as the SAFE programme and the development of web pages and resources dedicated to patient safety. Mr Bamber introduces the RCPCH patient safety portal, which offers a wealth of information including podcasts on safety culture, psychological safety, learning from harm, and addressing inequality in safety. He also details the launch of a safety e-bulletin, distributed to members every two months, summarizing the latest developments in paediatric patient safety. Mr Bamber encourages all members to engage with these resources and invites non-members to access previous editions via the RCPCH website. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: How paediatricians can work differently to improve care and wellbeing
summary: Four practical changes to paediatric working: rapid review clinics, early senior decisions, hospital at home and open-ended discharge plans for families.
description:
Professor Steve Turner shares concise insights on how paediatricians can work differently to enhance patient care and improve their own professional wellbeing. He emphasises that caring for patients and their families must remain central to paediatric practice. Key strategies he highlights include:

- Rapid review clinics to see children promptly during business hours, avoiding unnecessary overnight visits to tired paediatricians.

- Early involvement of senior decision-makers (ST4 level and above, including consultants) to reduce unnecessary tests and ineffective treatments, ensuring the right care is delivered at the right time and place.

- Hospital at home models, enabling more children to receive care in their own homes rather than in hospital, which requires a cultural shift for clinicians accustomed to hospital-based care.

- Improved discharge planning, providing support to families after hospital discharge to reduce unnecessary GP or emergency department visits. He advocates for open-ended discharge plans where parents can easily re-engage with paediatric services if needed.

Professor Turner’s reflections offer practical, patient-centered approaches to transform paediatric care delivery and support clinicians in their roles. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: RCPCH Conference: strategy, advocacy, and international impact

speakers.name: Professor Steve Turner
speakers.role: President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH)

summary: The four pillars of the RCPCH strategy: supporting members, advocating for children, using research and quality improvement, and expanding international impact.
description:
Professor Steve Turner, President of the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH), shares his goals for the RCPCH conference and outlines the College’s strategic direction. He emphasises the importance of lifelong learning, networking, and helping members understand the College’s role. Professor Turner details the four pillars of the RCPCH strategy, developed from extensive member feedback in 2024:

1) Supporting members working under challenging circumstances to help them fulfill their roles.

2) Advocating for children and young people, amplifying their voices in healthcare.

3) Using research and quality improvement to enhance patient care.

4) Expanding international impact, supporting members globally and advancing humanitarian work.

He highlights the College’s continued commitment to these priorities, ensuring both UK-based and international members are supported and that child health advocacy remains central to the College’s mission. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: The MAP study: understanding and improving mental health admissions to paediatric wards

speakers.name: Dr Lee Hudson
speakers.role: Clinical Associate Professor, UCL Institute of Child Health; Consultant General Paediatrician, Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: A NIHR-funded study of rising mental health admissions to general paediatric wards, using national data, surveillance and interviews to shape recommendations.
description: Dr Lee Hudson, Clinical Associate Professor, UCL Institute of Child Health; Consultant General Paediatrician, Great Ormond Street Hospital, introduces the MAP study (Mental Health Admissions to the Paediatric Ward), an NIHR-funded project based at University College London. The study responds to a marked rise in children admitted to general paediatric wards for acute mental health crises—a trend with little existing literature. Over the past decade, there has been a 65% increase in such admissions in England, with a particularly dramatic 500% rise among 11–15-year-old girls with eating disorders. The project comprises three work packages: analysis of national trends (recently published in The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health), a surveillance study with 15 hospitals to gather granular data on admissions, and qualitative interviews with young people, families, and staff to identify areas for improvement. The findings are being synthesised with input from major stakeholders, including the RCPCH, the Royal College of Psychiatrists, young people, and parents, to develop recommendations for better care both in the UK and internationally. Dr Hudson emphasises the urgent need for improved approaches, as mental health admissions to paediatric wards are increasing and require better support for both patients and staff. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Communicating medical research to patients and communities with creative digital media

speakers.name: Olivia Cottington
speakers.role: Honorary Clinical Public Engagement Coordinator at University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust

summary: How short digital stories and infographics shared on social media explain ongoing research to patients and families and gather their views on new treatments.
description: Olivia Cottington, Honorary Clinical Public Engagement Coordinator at University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, shares insights into her work focused on communicating medical research to patients and the wider community. Rather than acting as a clinical practitioner, Olivia is engaged in initiatives that use creative digital media—such as short digital stories and engaging infographics—to raise awareness about ongoing medical research and its potential benefits for patients and families. These resources are shared via social media to reach a broad audience and encourage feedback from patients and families about their views and experiences with research. The collected feedback is then presented at medical conferences to show professionals the appetite for integrating new treatments into standard care and to build support for making these treatments accessible across the UK. Olivia emphasises the importance of patient and public involvement in shaping research priorities and improving healthcare delivery. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Burosumab in paediatric practice: transforming treatment for X-linked hypophosphataemia
summary: How burosumab, a fortnightly injection, treats the cause of X-linked hypophosphataemia and compares with oral phosphate and vitamin D in clinical experience.
description: Dr Sanjay Gupta discusses the novel treatment for X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH), focusing on burosumab—a fully human monoclonal antibody that targets the underlying pathology of the disease. Traditionally, XLH has been managed with high doses of oral phosphate and activated vitamin D, treatments that are often challenging due to poor compliance, unpleasant taste, gastrointestinal side effects, and the need for daily administration. Burosumab, administered as a fortnightly subcutaneous injection, addresses the root cause by inhibiting excess fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF-23), which leads to phosphate loss in urine and reduced activated vitamin D levels. Dr Gupta shares his clinical experience, noting excellent tolerability in children treated with burosumab, normalisation of phosphate levels, improved bone health without the need for further corrective surgery, and significant reduction in bone pain—resulting in a marked improvement in quality of life. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Recognising and diagnosing X-linked hypophosphataemia in paediatric practice

speakers.name: Dr Sanjay Gupta
speakers.role: Consultant paediatrician at Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust

summary: Practical tips for spotting X-linked hypophosphataemia, including de novo cases and the range of professionals who may see affected children first.
description: Dr Sanjay Gupta, consultant paediatrician at Hull University Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust, discusses the importance of recognising rare diseases such as X-linked hypophosphataemia (XLH) in children. He emphasises that while a family history may raise suspicion for this X-linked dominant condition, up to 20–30% of cases are due to de novo mutations and may present to a variety of healthcare professionals—including dentists (for dental abscesses), neurosurgeons (for head shape deformities), orthopaedic surgeons, and paediatricians. These practical tips aim to improve early recognition and accurate diagnosis of XLH, ultimately enhancing care for affected children. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: The British Paediatric Surveillance Unit: a global model for rare disease research in children

speakers.name: Dr Peter Davis
speakers.role: Chair of the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit (BPSU)

summary: How the BPSU, set up in 1986 to study rare childhood diseases, became a model for surveillance units in other countries and supports collaboration.
description: Dr Peter Davis, Chair of the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit (BPSU), discusses the pioneering role of the BPSU in advancing the understanding of rare diseases in children. Established in 1986, the BPSU was created to study rare diseases, determine their incidence and prevalence, and assess outcomes for affected children. Over more than three decades, the BPSU has become a model for similar surveillance units worldwide, with Germany following in 1992, and Australia, New Zealand, and Canada subsequently establishing their own units. These international collaborations have generated a wealth of studies and publications, significantly enhancing global knowledge about rare diseases in children. Dr Davis highlights the BPSU’s ongoing commitment to supporting research, sharing best practices, and fostering international partnerships to improve outcomes for children with rare diseases. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Neonatal Oral Antibiotics at Home (NOAH) project: improving early discharge and family outcomes

speakers.name: Dr David Bartle
speakers.role: Royal Devon University Hospital

speakers.name: Dr Harriet Aughey
speakers.role: Royal Devon University Hospital

summary: A pilot letting newborns with suspected early-onset infection switch to oral antibiotics and go home sooner, with fewer bed days and no adverse events.
description: Dr David Bartle and Dr Harriet Aughey, Royal Devon University Hospital, present the Neonatal Oral Antibiotics at Home (NOAH) project. Inspired by the results of the RAIN study, which demonstrated the benefits of switching from intravenous to oral antibiotics in newborns and enabling earlier discharge, the NOAH project was developed to support babies with suspected early-onset infection who are eligible to switch to oral antibiotics. The project involved extensive collaboration with local infectious disease teams, maternity and neonatal safety initiatives, and partnerships such as the Maternity and Neonatal Safety Improvement Programme. Supported by the Health Innovation Network South West and PenARC, the pilot has yielded positive outcomes, including reduced hospital bed days, improved parental satisfaction, enhanced bonding, and better breastfeeding rates. Importantly, there have been no adverse events or cases of reinfection. The team is now planning a regional rollout and evaluation, with all project resources available for download to support implementation in other trusts. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Building research capacity and improving adolescent health through a multisectoral approach

speakers.name: Professor Dougal Hargreaves
speakers.role: Imperial College London

summary: Why child health research is under-funded, and how joined-up health, education and social care investment could improve outcomes for young people.
description: Professor Dougal Hargreaves, Imperial College London, discusses a project focused on building research capacity in under-researched areas of paediatrics and child health. He highlights a striking disparity: children and young people make up about 20% of the population and use 10% of NHS resources, yet receive only 5% of research funding. The project aims to increase investment in child health research to improve health outcomes and lifelong wellbeing. Professor Hargreaves particularly emphasises adolescent health, advocating for a more multisectoral and joined-up approach. He notes that young people do not see their physical health, mental health, educational experience, and social care as separate issues, but rather as interconnected parts of their lives. The current system is often fragmented, with young people receiving support from multiple services that are not well-coordinated. The project seeks to join up data, literature, and narratives to demonstrate the benefits of integrated investment in health and education, ultimately leading to better, more efficient, and cost-effective outcomes for young people. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Supporting trainee involvement in paediatric research: RCPCH Trainee Research Network

speakers.name: Dr Eva Wooding
speakers.role: Co-chair of the RCPCH Trainee Research Network (TRN) and academic clinical fellow in paediatrics

summary: How the Trainee Research Network helps trainees and the wider workforce get into research through regional reps, study days and a monthly online seminar.
description: Dr Eva Wooding, co-chair of the RCPCH Trainee Research Network (TRN) and academic clinical fellow in paediatrics, discusses the network’s mission to support trainees, resident doctors, and the wider paediatric workforce in becoming more involved with research. She highlights that research is essential for advancing child health and is valued by young people themselves. The college supports research engagement through local trainee representatives who help members discover research opportunities in their regions, as well as through national initiatives such as biannual study days—one entry-level and one advanced—open to all resident doctors, trust doctors, and the broader child health workforce. These events provide practical skills, boost CVs, and help participants understand the relevance of research to clinical practice. Additionally, the TRN offers a monthly online research seminar, ‘TREES’, on the last Tuesday of each month, which covers a wide range of topics and supports research competencies and portfolio development. Dr Wooding encourages anyone interested to explore the TRN section on the RCPCH website for more information and to reach out to the network with suggestions for future events. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Point-of-care ultrasound in neonatal and paediatric practice

speakers.name: Dr Bikash Bhojnagarwala
speakers.role: Consultant neonatologist with expertise in paediatric cardiology at Medway NHS Foundation Trust

summary: The role and limits of bedside point-of-care ultrasound, how it differs from specialist imaging, and the learning pathway for clinicians.
description: Dr Bikash Bhojnagarwala, consultant neonatologist with expertise in paediatric cardiology at Medway NHS Foundation Trust, discusses the evolving role of point-of-care ultrasound in neonatal and paediatric clinical settings. He highlights how point-of-care ultrasound has become a vital tool for making timely clinical decisions, especially for both neonatal and paediatric patients. Dr Bhojnagarwala emphasizes the importance of understanding the appropriate scope and limitations of this technology—encouraging clinicians to use it judiciously and in conjunction with other imaging modalities. He explains the distinction between bedside point-of-care ultrasound, which is performed by clinicians as part of their immediate patient assessment, and more detailed echocardiography or imaging performed by specialist sonographers or radiologists for objective reporting. Dr Bhojnagarwala outlines the learning pathway for clinicians, starting with image acquisition, progressing to interpretation, and ultimately integrating findings to supplement clinical decision-making. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: RCPCH Wales manifesto: prioritising child health

speakers.name: Dr Nick Wilkinson
speakers.role: Officer for Wales at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH)

speakers.name: Dr Dana Beasley
speakers.role: Deputy Officer for Wales

summary: The RCPCH Wales manifesto ahead of the 2026 Senedd elections, its four priorities, and the pressures on child health and the workforce in Wales.
description: Dr Nick Wilkinson, Officer for Wales at the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH), and Dr Dana Beasley, Deputy Officer for Wales, discuss the launch of the RCPCH Wales manifesto in anticipation of the 2026 Senedd elections. They highlight the significant deterioration in the health and well-being of children and young people in Wales, marked by rising obesity, worsening mental health, and widening health inequalities. The paediatric workforce is described as tired, stretched, and at risk of burnout due to chronic underinvestment and lack of funding, resulting in some of the poorest child health outcomes in Europe. The manifesto outlines four core priorities: empowering the child health workforce, transforming children’s health services, embracing data and digital innovation, and tackling inequalities to deliver for all children. Dr Wilkinson and Dr Beasley call on all politicians to commit to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and invite engagement to help transform children’s services in Wales. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Optimising postoperative care for elective spinal surgery in paediatrics: a Belfast perspective

speakers.name: Dr Thomas Dowling
speakers.role: Paediatric registrar at Belfast Health and Social Care Trust

summary: An audit of elective spinal surgery patients in Belfast suggests many do not need intensive care afterwards, and the case for a paediatric high dependency unit.
description: Dr Thomas Dowling, paediatric registrar at Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, presents findings from an audit on elective spinal surgery patients in Belfast, focusing on the need for postoperative paediatric intensive care. The study reviewed two years of cases involving 42 patients and found that only three required level two or three interventions—those typically associated with paediatric intensive or high dependency care. Most patients had minimal intervention needs, suggesting that many could be managed safely on the ward rather than in intensive care. Dr Dowling highlights the unique challenge in Northern Ireland, where there is currently no dedicated high dependency unit; as a result, patients who might otherwise be managed in such a setting are admitted to paediatric intensive care. He discusses ongoing efforts to review existing guidelines, adapt care environments, and work with stakeholders to develop and demonstrate the need for a paediatric high dependency unit in the region. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Evolution and challenges in neonatal MRI: a 15-year retrospective analysis

speakers.name: Dr Melinda Vlad
speakers.role: East Kent Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

summary: How neonatal brain MRI use has changed over 15 years, why many images are still suboptimal, and the steps proposed to improve scanning.
description: Dr Melinda Vlad, East Kent Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, discusses the evolving role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in the care of newborn babies at risk of brain injuries. She highlights the challenges of obtaining high-quality images due to the need for babies to remain still during scans and the time required for adequate imaging. Dr Vlad presents findings from a project comparing current MRI processes with those from 15 years ago, using electronic patient records and standardized MRI reporting. Key results include a significant shift in indications, with 20% of recent scans performed for antenatally diagnosed brain abnormalities—reflecting advances in fetal medicine. The study also found a 700% increase in monthly MRI scans, attributed to changes in neonatal management and evolving evidence supporting MRI’s prognostic value. However, about 40% of images remain suboptimal, impacting both clinical information for families and resource utilization. Dr Vlad outlines next steps to standardize imaging processes, optimize sedation, advocate for longer MRI slots, and increase scanner availability to meet growing demand. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: CoLab: improving care for children with medical complexity through partnership and innovation

speakers.name: Dr Mary Salama
speakers.role: Consultant paediatrician at Birmingham Children’s Hospital

summary: A free partnership connecting professionals, carers and families to share ideas and develop new approaches to care for children with medical complexity.
description:
https://www.colabpartnership.org.uk/

Dr Mary Salama, consultant paediatrician at Birmingham Children’s Hospital, introduces CoLab—a partnership initiative dedicated to improving care for children with medical complexity. These children represent a vulnerable group and are high users of healthcare services in both community and acute settings. CoLab aims to connect professionals, carers, and families to share ideas, learn from each other, and collaboratively develop new approaches to care. Dr Salama highlights the free, open nature of the initiative and invites all interested parties to participate in open mic sessions and upcoming events, including a “dragon’s den” where experienced parent carers will provide feedback on new ideas. She encourages attendees to join the initiative, share their insights, and help drive meaningful improvements for children with complex medical needs. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Meaningful co-production with young people: shaping healthcare solutions

speakers.name: Dr Mary Salama
speakers.role: Consultant paediatrician at Birmingham Children’s Hospital

summary: How young people from inner-city Birmingham schools researched community health issues, and how systems thinking was applied to their findings.
description: Dr Mary Salama, consultant paediatrician at Birmingham Children’s Hospital, discusses her project focused on merging meaningful co-production with young people and systems thinking in healthcare improvement. She highlights the use of symbolic pink glasses to signify this collaborative approach, building on previous years’ pink hats. The project engaged young people from inner-city Birmingham schools to research health and community issues, with students conducting community research and sharing their findings. Dr Salama and her team then applied a human factors or ergonomic filter to this data, using systems thinking to identify emerging themes and inform improvements. The goal is to refine these tools and feedback the findings to enhance the systems supporting young people in their communities. Dr Salama emphasises the importance of involving young people in shaping healthcare solutions and using scientific methods to address inequalities within the system. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Digital and animated medicine information for children: enhancing engagement and adherence

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: A project giving children animated, translated information about their medicines through QR codes on pharmacy labels, shaped by children to aid adherence.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital, discusses a pioneering project focused on delivering dynamic, animated, and digitally translated information about medicines directly to children. The initiative recognises that engaging children with information about their medicines improves adherence, yet there is currently very little material that truly captures their interest. Steve highlights the added challenge for those who cannot read or who speak other languages. The project is exploring the use of digital, animated content that can be accessed via QR codes placed on pharmacy labels. Extensive patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) work is underway, with children actively shaping the content—determining which aspects of medicine information are most important and relevant to them. The goal is to balance what children want to know with what healthcare professionals believe they need to know, ultimately improving long-term engagement and adherence. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: RCPCH and NPPG Joint Medicines Committee

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital and Chair of the Joint Medicines Committee

summary: How the multi-professional Joint Medicines Committee works to solve problems, lobby for change and prioritise safety in paediatric medicines.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital and Chair of the Joint Medicines Committee, provides insights into the unique structure and influence of this multi-professional committee. The committee is a collaboration between the Royal College and the Neonatal and Paediatric Pharmacists Group, and includes representatives from organizations such as the BNF, MHRA, and ABPI. Steve highlights that the committee is not limited to a single issue but is instrumental in addressing current challenges, lobbying for change, and solving complex problems, such as those arising from coroners’ Regulation 28 cases. He emphasises the importance of both developing solutions and ensuring their implementation, noting that consensus and multi-professional perspectives are central to the committee’s effectiveness. Steve also reflects on the committee’s legacy, including the creation of the BNF for Children and Medicines for Children, and states that current priorities are firmly focused on safety in paediatric medicines. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Standardising paediatric medicine labels to enhance safety and clarity

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: Why dose wording on pharmacy labels varies, why parents prefer millilitres, and the push to standardise liquid medicine labels to reduce errors.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital, discusses the challenges and solutions around the labelling of paediatric medicines. The video highlights the significant variability in how doses are written on pharmacy labels—some use milligrams, others millilitres, and some a combination of both—leading to confusion for parents and carers. Steve explains that while legal requirements for pharmacy labelling exist, the level of detail is not specified, resulting in inconsistent practices. He emphasises that the most important factor is consistency: all labels should be written the same way, regardless of the chosen format. However, research shows that parents prefer doses to be written in millilitres, as this is the unit they use when administering the medicine. Steve details ongoing efforts to standardise paediatric medicine labels, including a forthcoming position statement from the Neonatal and Paediatric Pharmacy Group, and discussions with regulators to establish national standards. The primary recommendation is that all liquid medicines should display the dose in millilitres, simplifying administration and reducing the risk of errors. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Standardising liquid medicine strengths to improve paediatric medication safety

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: Why the many concentrations of liquid medicines confuse families, and the case for one or two standard strengths per medicine to simplify dosing.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital, discusses the challenge of multiple liquid medicine strengths and the importance of standardization in paediatric medication safety. The discussion highlights that, despite a move toward using tablets in children whenever possible, liquid medicines remain widely used and often come in a confusing array of concentrations—sometimes up to 14 different strengths for a single medicine. Tomlin explains that this variability leads to confusion for parents and carers, who may receive different strengths from various pharmacies or hospital departments. He advocates for standardizing to just one or two strengths for each liquid medicine, suitable for all ages from neonates to adults. The goal of this approach is to simplify dosing, reduce errors, and ultimately improve safety. Tomlin also details ongoing efforts to create a formulary of recommended concentrations and encourages the industry to support this standardization by licensing fewer strengths. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Improving safety and standardisation in paediatric IV infusions

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: Evidence of inaccurate ward-prepared syringes and the case for a few standard IV infusion concentrations, smart pumps and ready-made syringes.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital, provides insights into the challenges and solutions for improving the accuracy and safety of intravenous (IV) infusions in paediatric care. The discussion highlights the significant inaccuracies found in ward-level syringe preparation—with studies showing that 68% of syringes are outside a 7–12% accuracy range and 28% are more than 20% inaccurate. Steve emphasises that such variability would be unacceptable for most medicines, yet it remains common practice in paediatrics. He advocates for standardization of IV infusion concentrations across the paediatric population, noting that for most drugs, only about five standard concentrations are needed to cover all ages and weights, including neonates. Tomlin also discusses the benefits of smart pumps and ready-made syringes, which can further improve accuracy and safety. He concludes that it is time to move forward and implement these changes to ensure children receive the correct doses of IV medications. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Medicine sustainability in paediatrics: reducing carbon footprints in child healthcare

speakers.name: Steve Tomlin
speakers.role: Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital

summary: How paediatric teams can cut the carbon footprint of medicines, for example by moving children from liquids to tablets and from IV to oral treatment.
description: Steve Tomlin, Director of the Children’s Medicines Research & Innovation Centre at Great Ormond Street Hospital, provides insights into the importance of medicine sustainability in paediatrics. The discussion highlights that while much of the NHS carbon footprint from medicines is linked to industry, paediatric medicine has specific considerations that can make a real difference. Tomlin explains that 25% of the NHS carbon footprint is attributable to medicines, and while much of this is outside direct clinician control, there are practical steps that paediatric teams can take to reduce environmental impact. Research shows that liquid medicines have a carbon footprint about 40 times higher than tablets in terms of administration, and oral medicines are far better than intravenous (IV) routes. Tomlin encourages clinicians to transition children from liquids to tablets, and to review IV therapies for opportunities to switch to oral medications, as these changes can significantly reduce the carbon footprint associated with paediatric medicine. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: AI-driven multimodal data processing for early detection of ADHD and depression in children

speakers.name: Dr Mohsen Naqvi
speakers.role: Senior Associate Professor (Reader) in Signal Processing and AI at Newcastle University

summary: Research on AI tools that analyse video, audio and questionnaires to help clinicians detect ADHD and depression in children earlier.
description: Dr Mohsen Naqvi, Senior Associate Professor (Reader) in Signal Processing and AI at Newcastle University, provides insights into interdisciplinary research at the intersection of engineering and medicine, focusing on the development of artificial intelligence tools for mental health detection in children. The discussion highlights the use of multimodal data—including video, audio, behavioural observations, and digital questionnaires—to create computer-based applications capable of identifying conditions such as ADHD and depression. Dr Naqvi explains how these tools aim to support clinicians by automating aspects of the diagnostic process, leveraging the widespread use of smart devices among children. He emphasises the importance of close collaboration between engineers and clinicians to ensure that AI solutions are both effective and clinically relevant, with the ultimate goal of developing accessible applications to help detect mental health issues early. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Using virtual reality simulation to improve hospital care for children with autism spectrum disorder

speakers.name: Roshni Das
speakers.role: Medical student at King’s College London

summary: Early evidence that virtual reality simulation training improves clinicians' skills and confidence with autistic children, and plans for larger studies.
description: Roshni Das, a medical student at King’s College London, provides insights into her research focused on improving the management of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in hospital settings. The discussion highlights the challenges paediatricians face when caring for children with ASD and introduces a novel solution: virtual reality (VR)-based simulation training for clinicians. Initial findings indicate that VR training enhances clinicians’ skills, confidence, and competence in managing these patients. However, Roshni notes the current evidence base is limited by small sample sizes and inconsistent protocols. To address this, she advocates for large-scale studies and the establishment of a national registry to improve training processes. Roshni outlines plans for a large audit across multiple hospitals and the inclusion of focus groups with clinicians, patients, and parents to further evaluate the benefits of VR-based training. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Neotree: optimising newborn care and survival in low-resource settings

speakers.name: Professor Michelle Heys
speakers.role: UCL Great Ormond Street Institute for Child Health

summary: An overview of Neotree, which combines real-time data with community voices to support newborn care and survival in low-resource settings.
description: Professor Michelle Heys, UCL Great Ormond Street Institute for Child Health, an overview of Neotree, a project optimising newborn care and survival in low-resource settings. The approach to improving outcomes for newborns in these settings focuses on the integration of real-time data with community voices to support more effective and contextually relevant clinical decision-making. By leveraging timely health information and local insights, this model aims to strengthen health system responsiveness and equity, ultimately improving neonatal care and survival. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, UK.

title: 40 years of impact: the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit (BPSU)

speakers.name: Dr Ifeanyichukwu Okike
speakers.role: Deputy Chair of the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit and honorary professor

summary: How four decades of BPSU studies have shaped screening, policy and safety initiatives, and how the unit is working to sustain clinician participation.
description: Dr Ifeanyichukwu Okike, Deputy Chair of the British Paediatric Surveillance Unit and honorary professor, provides insights into the profound impact of BPSU studies on child health over the past four decades. The discussion highlights how BPSU research has shaped health policy and clinical practice, with landmark studies influencing the utilization of liver centers, national screening programs for metabolic and endocrine disorders such as MCAD and congenital hypothyroidism, and patient safety initiatives—including investigations into the unexpected collapse of babies in postnatal wards. Dr Okike also discusses the critical role of BPSU studies during health emergencies, notably the COVID-19 pandemic, where findings informed public health messaging and management strategies. He acknowledges current challenges, including declining awareness among trainees and lower clinician response rates, and outlines ongoing efforts to embed BPSU participation in training curricula to sustain its legacy and maximize future impact. Dr Okike emphasizes the importance of translating research into policy to ensure that patients benefit directly from surveillance and research activities. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: National standardisation of paediatric early warning systems and their impact on care

speakers.name: Professor Damian Roland
speakers.role: Consultant in paediatric emergency medicine and honorary professor at Leicester Hospitals and University of Leicester

summary: How a national paediatric early warning system was introduced in the UK, its uptake, and the SPOT pilot extending it to emergency departments and the community.
description: Professor Damian Roland, consultant in paediatric emergency medicine and honorary professor at Leicester Hospitals and University of Leicester, provides insights into the development and implementation of national standardised paediatric early warning systems (PEWS) in the UK. The discussion highlights how, for many years, hospitals used a variety of PEWS, leading to confusion and inconsistency when clinicians moved between settings. In response, NHS England, the RCPCH, and the RCN collaborated to create a national program, resulting in the release of a standardised PEWS in late 2023. Currently, 60% of hospitals are either using the new system or are in the process of implementing it. Professor Roland also describes an exciting pilot program extending PEWS into emergency departments and, ultimately, into the wider community as part of the SPOT (Systemwide Paediatric Observation Tracking) initiative. This will enable all healthcare professionals to communicate about a child’s condition using a common language, improving safety and continuity of care. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Impact of gene therapy on respiratory status in children with spinal muscular atrophy

speakers.name: Dr Yeliz Koc
speakers.role: Paediatric pulmonologist at Medipol University Hospital

summary: A study of 160 children with spinal muscular atrophy type 1 shows how Zolgensma gene therapy affected their need for respiratory and ventilatory support.
description: Dr Yeliz Koc, paediatric pulmonologist at Medipol University Hospital, provides insights into a study evaluating the effectiveness of Zolgensma gene therapy on the respiratory status of children with spinal muscular atrophy type 1. The discussion highlights the analysis of 160 patients, comparing their respiratory outcomes before and after gene therapy, and dividing the cohort into two groups: children below two years and those older than two years. Dr Koc explains that, while there was no statistically significant change in invasive mechanical ventilation requirements after therapy, the need for respiratory support decreased, and a greater number of patients became independent of invasive ventilation. Additionally, the study tracked the number of patients able to achieve spontaneous breathing after gene therapy. Dr Koc emphasises the clinical importance of these findings and suggests the need for further randomized controlled trials to confirm the results. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Impact of point-of-care testing for Group A Streptococcus in the paediatric emergency department

speakers.name: Dr Alison Kemp
speakers.role: Warrington Hospital

speakers.name: Dr Connie Foxhall
speakers.role: Warrington Hospital

summary: An audit finds point-of-care testing for Group A Streptococcus shortened waits and lowered antibiotic prescribing in a paediatric emergency department.
description: Dr Alison Kemp and Dr Connie Foxhall, Warrington Hospital, provide insights into a retrospective audit evaluating the implementation of point-of-care testing for Group A Streptococcus in the paediatric emergency department. The discussion highlights the analysis of 82 children randomly selected between November 2023 and February 2024, focusing on antibiotic prescription rates, reattendance, and length of stay. The findings showed that children who received point-of-care testing had a significantly shorter average wait time (186 minutes) compared to those who did not (317 minutes). Antibiotic prescription rates were lower among tested children, supporting improved antimicrobial stewardship and reduced clinician bias in decision-making. Drs Kemp and Foxhall emphasise that point-of-care testing enhances patient care by lowering wait times, reducing unnecessary admissions and readmissions, and supporting timely, evidence-based treatment. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Local extubation in children with status epilepticus

speakers.name: Dr Kokul Sriskandarajah
speakers.role: Chelsea and Westminster Hospital

summary: How teaching on transport service guidelines allowed a district general hospital to extubate children with status epilepticus locally and avoid PICU transfers.
description: Dr Kokul Sriskandarajah, Chelsea and Westminster Hospital, provides insights into a project focused on improving the management of children with status epilepticus at a busy district general hospital in London. The discussion highlights a study conducted both prospectively and retrospectively, following the introduction of new guidelines for local extubation in children who require intubation due to prolonged seizures. Dr Sriskandarajah describes how, prior to guideline implementation, nine children could not be extubated locally due to a lack of clinician knowledge and awareness of the guidelines. After targeted teaching and discussion of the Children’s Acute Transport Service guidelines, the team was able to safely extubate two children locally, thereby avoiding unnecessary transfers to paediatric intensive care and conserving valuable PICU beds in London. He emphasizes that this approach can be adopted by other trusts, supporting safe, local extubation for children with status epilepticus and improving resource utilization. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Improving confidence in paediatric dermatology management in the emergency department

speakers.name: Dr Yasmin Mahfouz
speakers.role: Evelina London Children’s Hospital

summary: A tailored skin conditions guideline for a children's A&E department, with escalation pathways and diverse images, raised clinician confidence by over 70%.
description: Dr Yasmin Mahfouz, Evelina London Children’s Hospital, provides insights into a project aimed at addressing the confidence gap among clinicians managing dermatological presentations in a busy children’s A&E department. The discussion highlights how, despite dermatology not being a 24-hour service, children frequently present to A&E with new or worsening skin conditions. Dr Mahfouz describes the development of a tailored guideline, created in collaboration with dermatology colleagues and informed by a survey of common presentations and clinician knowledge gaps. The guideline includes management plans, escalation pathways, and representative images of children from diverse backgrounds. Following implementation, clinician confidence in managing paediatric dermatology presentations improved by more than 70%. Dr Mahfouz emphasises the importance of identifying knowledge gaps, developing targeted resources, and continuously seeking to improve care for children with dermatological conditions. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Recognising and managing skin conditions in children on biologic therapies

speakers.name: Dr Tess McPherson
speakers.role: Paediatric dermatologist at Oxford University Hospitals

summary: Skin problems are an expected complication of biologic therapies in some young people; early recognition and joint work with dermatologists help manage them.
description: Dr Tess McPherson, a leading paediatric dermatologist at Oxford University Hospitals, provides insights into the latest research and development in the recognition and management of skin conditions in children and young people receiving biologic therapies for inflammatory conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease. The discussion highlights the increasing prevalence of significant skin problems among patients treated with biologics—previously described as paradoxical psoriasis, but now recognized as an expected complication in a proportion of young people. Dr McPherson emphasises the importance of early recognition, patient counselling about potential skin issues, and collaborative management with dermatologists, which may involve topical treatments or adjustments to medication. She also discusses how these findings are improving our understanding of immune pathway alterations caused by new medications and the need for multidisciplinary teamwork to inform and support patients and families. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Sleep disordered breathing in children with neuromuscular disorders

speakers.name: Professor Nitin Kapur
speakers.role: President, Paediatric & Child Health Division, Royal Australasian College of Physicians

summary: Why clinicians should keep a low threshold for detecting sleep-disordered breathing in children with neuromuscular disorders to prevent serious harm.
description: Professor Nitin Kapur; President, Paediatric & Child Health Division, Royal Australasian College of Physicians, highlights the critical importance of maintaining a low threshold for the early detection of sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) in children with neuromuscular disorders. Early recognition and intervention can prevent significant morbidity and mortality, improve quality of life, and support better long-term outcomes for affected children and their families. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Inspiring a culture of patient safety

speakers.name: Dr Peter Lachman
speakers.role: Lead Faculty for Quality Improvement at the RCPI (Royal College of Physicians of Ireland)

summary: The case for making patient safety a core part of medical training and daily hospital practice, rather than something taught reactively after graduation.
description:
Dr Peter Lachman, Lead Faculty for Quality Improvement at the RCPI (Royal College of Physicians of Ireland), shares his expert perspective on embedding a culture of safety within medical education and clinical practice. Drawing on decades of experience in patient safety, he emphasises the importance of making patient safety a core element of medical training, rather than a reactive concept introduced after graduation. Dr Lachman advocates for proactive, habitual safety practices in hospitals, and calls for a significant transformation in the design of medical education and healthcare systems to ensure safety is prioritised every day. This approach has the potential to improve outcomes for both patients and staff and to raise standards of care on a global scale. This interview took place at the RCPCH conference 2025 in Glasgow, Scotland.
